rationale: B wins by a nose because its strongest angle makes the disclosed number the story instead of treating it as arithmetic homework: "Substack says its top creators split more than $400M last year — and won't say how the split works." A's equivalent, "What Substack's $400M creator number says about Substack's own revenue," is solid, but narrower and less likely to make a skeptical reporter lean forward. B still needs its overclaims sanded down; the Mailchimp/YouTube line is cute enough to be dangerous.
gaps_in_A: "One writer's case for moving video and podcasts onto Substack under a 10% cut" is a kept angle before the needed protagonist exists; the set admits it needs "a named Substack writer," so this should be conditional, not presented as ready.
"the moment writers see video in their subscribers' feeds" invents a surface the update did not give; "TikTok-style feed" is not the same as subscribers' feeds or a ranked penalty for text.
"Next step: `meanest-editor`" is process noise. For landing press, the next move is journalist-fit plus proof collection, not another roast.
"Substack is done being a newsletter company" is a little too absolute; the facts support a category question, not a completed identity change.
gaps_in_B: "Substack has stopped competing with Mailchimp and started competing with YouTube" invents a clean competitor swap the update never supplied; use it as an editor's question, not a fact.

"the people who chose Substack precisely because it was text now face a feed that rewards something they didn't sign up to make" assumes pressure and algorithmic reward. The proof list asks the right question, but the angle states the answer too early.
"Video hosting is one of the most expensive infrastructure commitments a platform can make" may be true, but it is outside the fact block. Source it or move it to proof needed.
"won't say how the split works" converts "not disclosed" into refusal. That is sharper copy, but it is a fact-risk trap.
